  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Marcus had always been the kind of person who managed things quietly and efficiently — the one in the server room at 2 a.m. when a database crashed, methodical and calm under pressure. At thirty-five, he had built a life around predictability: clean data structures, scheduled backups, controlled outcomes. Then, in the winter of that year, he developed what he initially dismissed as a persistent chest infection. By the time he was admitted to the emergency department, his oxygen saturation had dropped dangerously low, and he was diagnosed with a severe bilateral pneumonia that progressed rapidly to respiratory failure. For eleven days he lay in an ICU bed, a nasal cannula replaced by a non-rebreather mask, then by high-flow oxygen. He watched nurses adjust IV drips above his arm, felt the cold slide of a needle each time a blood draw was ordered, and endured the particular helplessness of not being able to draw a full breath while clinicians leaned over him with stethoscopes and pulse oximeters. His then-wife, sitting beside him on the third day, had been told quietly in the corridor that the situation was serious. Marcus had heard enough of that conversation to understand what serious meant. What stayed with him from those eleven days was not any single moment but a texture of sustained horror — the low-oxygen warning light casting its red pulse across the ceiling, the mechanical rhythm of the oxygen equipment, the knowledge that his body was doing something he could not stop or negotiate with.

He was discharged six weeks later, lungs scarred but functional. In the months that followed, the world did not feel the way it had before. His body, which had once been a neutral instrument he relied on without thinking, had become something he monitored constantly. He was certain, in a way he could not argue himself out of, that it would fail him again without warning, and that next time there would be no recovery. What frightened him most was not death in the abstract but the specific sensation of breathlessness — the memory of that suffocating tightness lived somewhere beneath conscious thought, and any hint of it in his chest now sent a wave of fear through him that felt indistinguishable from the original emergency. He had come to believe that a racing heart or tightening lungs were not normal fluctuations but early signals of catastrophe. Alongside the fear ran something darker and less manageable: a low, persistent anger at his own body, at the sheer arbitrariness of what had happened to him. He had done nothing wrong. He had been healthy, careful, unremarkable in his habits — and still his lungs had simply stopped working. That felt, in some register he could not fully articulate, like a betrayal he had not deserved and could not forgive. There was shame in it too, a corrosive kind — shame at having been reduced to helplessness in front of his wife, at having needed strangers to manage his most basic functions, at the fact that he could not simply recover and move on the way he felt he should have been able to.

Over the following year, Marcus reorganised his life around managing these signals. He stopped exercising entirely, convinced that the exertion would bring on the breathlessness he dreaded. He began restricting what he ate, monitoring his diet with the same granular attention he brought to database queries, finding that the sense of control over intake was one of the few things that quieted the background hum of physical unease. He cancelled a routine dental appointment, then a follow-up with his pulmonologist, then another. Hospitals, ambulances glimpsed from the road, even the antiseptic smell of a pharmacy — all of it had become intolerable. He rerouted his commute to avoid the street where the hospital stood.

At work, where he spent long hours alone in front of screens, the avoidance was easier to maintain. But the cost accumulated. His divorce, finalised eight months after his discharge, had been shaped in part by his withdrawal — his ex-wife had described living with someone who had become unreachable, sealed off. He had not contested her characterisation, though privately he felt a guilt about it that he had no idea what to do with — a sense that his inability to recover properly had cost her something she had not signed up to lose. Colleagues noticed that he declined team lunches and avoided the office first-aid room, once leaving a meeting abruptly when a colleague mentioned a recent surgery. His manager had begun asking questions.

When Marcus finally sought help, it was because of a moment at his desk. A routine system alert had caused his screen to flash red — the same colour as the low-oxygen warning light he remembered from the ICU monitor — and he had found himself unable to breathe properly for nearly twenty minutes, hands gripping the edge of his keyboard, certain something was happening to him. A colleague had called building security. The incident left him shaken and, underneath that, deeply ashamed — ashamed in a way that cut closer than the earlier humiliation, because it confirmed a fear he had been carrying quietly for months: that whatever had broken in him during those eleven days in the ICU was not getting better on its own. He arrived at the intake appointment guarded and precise in his language, as though clinical accuracy might create some distance from the material. He said he was not sure therapy could help with something that felt so physical. What he was most afraid of, he admitted after a long pause, was that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for his body to betray him again. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to stop.
